reason: MAX_LEN is 4,294,967,295 (the largest value a 4-byte length header can hold). Exercising this boundary for real requires constructing and validating an array of that size, which is not a practical thing to do in a test suite (multi-gigabyte allocation, minutes of runtime). The off-by-one at a boundary no realistic caller can reach is a real but untestable-in-practice gap; the header format's own 4-byte width is the actual documented limit.

Equivalent by construction: framed.length is always padded to a multiple of 3 (encode pads exactly for this), and base is always i*3 for integer i, so base is always a multiple of 3 too. base+1 is therefore always congruent to 1 mod 3, while framed.length is always congruent to 0 mod 3 -- they can never be exactly equal, so base+1 < framed.length and base+1 <= framed.length always agree on every reachable input.

Same invariant as the base+1 case one line above: base is always a multiple of 3 and framed.length is always a multiple of 3 (encode pads to ensure it), so base+2 is always congruent to 2 mod 3 and can never equal framed.length exactly. < and <= agree on every reachable input.

roundTrips() always calls decode() on the exact grid its own preceding encode() call just produced. encode()'s output is proven decodable by every other test in this suite (round-trip tests, the fuzz test, the explicit value-by-value check) -- this branch only fires if encode() itself produces a grid its own decode() cannot read, which is exactly the invariant the other 40+ tests already gate directly. It is a real defensive check (guards a future refactor that breaks that pairing), not dead code, but it cannot be exercised by any valid `bytes` argument today without first breaking encode/decode's own tested correctness.
